notes.1ai: Nearly all candidates were able to calculate the concentration of vitamin C in test-tube C . Occasionally a value of 75% was given instead of 0.75%. Some candidates appear to find percentage values less than 1% quite challenging. It is also important that values of less than one have a zero before the decimal point, i.e. 0.75 rather than .75.
notes.1aii: Most candidates were able to produce a suitable table of results, with a sufficient number of values that were correctly transcribed from the figure. Units (drops) were commonly written within the body of the table, resulting in a mark being missed. Although results for trial 1 and trial 2 were usually recorded, an average was sometimes missing despite being asked for in the question. A few candidates calculated the average incorrectly, or more commonly, found the average of the test- tubes rather than the average of the trials. This highlights the importance of reading the question carefully.
notes.1aiii: Most candidates could state a conclusion for the student’s results. Some answers were too vague or they simply described the results. Answers such as, it goes up with more vitamin C, is insufficient as both variables need to be included in the conclusion. The word ‘it’ should be avoided wherever possible. Similarly, stating that ‘D took 22 drops to become clear’ is a description rather than a conclusion.
notes.1aiv: Almost all candidates gave a good reason for repeating the investigation. The reason for doing repeats was to identify anomalies or to compare the values from each of the trials to see if they were consistent.
notes.1av: Many candidates were able to estimate a value for drink H which was in line with the results in 1(a)(ii) . Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0610 Biology June 2021
notes.1avi: Candidates were asked to provide two improvements that would allow for a more precise estimation of the concentration of vitamin C in drink H . Many answers were too vague and did not gain credit.
notes.1avii: Candidates were asked to identify two variables that were kept constant. Candidates should avoid writing amount, which in this case could mean concentration or volume of vitamin C or DCPIP. Candidates should specify exactly which quantity they mean (volume of vitamin C or concentration of DCPIP) or state the actual volume or concentration that was used.
notes.1b: This question was generally well answered with many candidates recognising that the size of the drops could vary. Some candidates confused volume with concentration and did not gain credit.
notes.1c: Candidates were asked to recall the tests for proteins and glucose. It was clear that many candidates were unfamiliar with tests using biuret and Benedict’s reagents.
notes.2ai: A large number of drawings included broken lines or shaded images. Care needed to be taken when drawing the detail of the leaf shape and the pattern of venation needed to be recorded accurately.
notes.2aii: Candidates were asked to draw a line on their drawing showing where they took the measurement for the leaf width. The majority did this well but a few omitted the line or drew a line that did not coincide with the width of the leaf. All measurements must be in either millimetres or centimetres (inches are not acceptable). Most candidates were able to calculate the magnification correctly although a small number inverted the equation.
notes.2bi: The quality of the graph was very high for many candidates. Some key points to consider when drawing graphs: • Labels on the axes should be complete and include units where appropriate. • Axes do not have to start at zero, but when they do not, this needs to be indicated. • Plotted points must be small, a small cross or circled dot is ideal. • A line of best fit can be a straight line or a curved line, depending on the data. In many cases, joining the plotted points with straight lines is sufficient, unless a line of best fit is specifically asked for. • Lines of best fit should not show extrapolation unless specifically asked for in the question.
notes.2bii: As with Question 1(a)(iii) , both variables needed to be mentioned when stating a conclusion. Simply saying that the lines goes up is not adequate for a mark.
notes.2biii: Generally, candidates performed well on this calculation of the rate of photosynthesis. The difference between one significant figure and one decimal place needs to be emphasised to candidates, as an answer of 2.8 bubbles per minute was commonly seen.
notes.2biv: Most candidates could identify the independent variable.
notes.2c: Some candidates found this question demanding. When writing plans, candidates should remember to: • state the independent variable and explain how this variable is changed, in this case moving a lamp further from the plant • identify the dependent variable and describe how it is to be measured, in this case collecting the volume of gas produced in a set time • identify the factors which need to be kept constant, in this case temperature, pH and concentration of carbon dioxide • state that there needs to be at least two repeats (three trials in total).
